articles.title: Chinese Martial Arts Curriculum
articles.summary: Chinese martial arts developed into many styles with many curriculums. Although it seems to have plenty of information, the curriculum is actually composed of just three types of trainings.
articles.content:
I. Introduction

Chinese martial arts developed into many styles with many curriculums. Although it seems to have plenty of information, the curriculum is actually composed of just three types of trainings. They are martial art forms training, martial art combat simulations training, and supplementary and fundamentals trainings exercises commonly known as gong exercises training. The objective of supplementary gong exercise training is for the quality of martial offensive and defensive maneuvers proficiency. The objective of the fundamentals gong exercise training is for the technical proficiency. The martial art forms training includes the bare hand forms, weapon forms, partner bare hand forms and partner weapon forms. Among the martial art combat simulations training, there are kicking, punching, fist striking, palm striking, grappling and wrestling techniques in solo drill and partner drill. Included in the gong exercises training, based on the objectives, are nei gong (internal work), wai gong (external work), rou gong (soft work), shang gong (light work) and yin gong (hard work). They are commonly referred to as empty training and heavily training. Generally, it is this last group of supplementary gong exercise training that determine the practitioners’ martial art combat skill and body conditioning.

By “martial art”, what does it mean? Literally, it is the art of war. Martial confrontation generally consists of competition involving power, technique, timing and strategy. The outcome of such a confrontation will be determined by number of factors. They include: which party is stronger, has more endurance, has a more powerful and speedy strike, is more familiar with and able to utilize techniques correctly and properly, and is more able to seize the opponent’s opening or weakness as an opportunity to launch a counterstrike. Therefore, one can see that victory in a martial art confrontation is determined by how much preparation a practitioner has made.

Although all Chinese martial arts systems and styles today borrowed training methods and techniques from each other to improve the quality of their systems to prepare their practitioners, traditionally, a complete system must have the three categories of training described above to prepare the practitioners. A typical system begins the students with the gong exercises training for fundamentals and follows up with the bare hand form to understand the features of the system. Then follow the martial art combat simulations training to understand the offensive and defensive techniques one learned and derived from the forms. The last program a student learns is the supplementary exercises from the gong exercises training again. The training guarantees the quality of the offensive and defensive techniques. In the past, practitioners have to go to great length to learn or to practice the supplementary gong exercises. There are many supplementary gong exercises training exercises available. It has the exercise for the beginning to the advance students. It has empty training exercise focus on the essence, qi and spirit and the heavy training exercise focus on the bones, muscles, ligaments, and sinews. The common exercise in the empty training is the different types of meditation exercises and the two most common exercises among the heavy training exercises are the Ba Duan Jing (Eight Pieces of Brocade) and Yi Jin Jing (Changing the Ligaments, tendons, sinews and vessels Exercise), among the Chinese martial art practitioners.

Ba Duan Jin is a Daoyin (dao means manipulation the body and its parts and yin means leading or guiding the qi) principle exercise. It is a very simple to do and has a very effective health benefit exercise. For a long time, ancient Chinese practiced it as a form of health maintenance exercise. It is the cream of the crop among the traditional Chinese cultivation culture exercises. Due to its simplicity and benefit, it practiced by many people and it had been developed into many variations. Although there are many variations available today, it is generally divided into sitting form and standing form. The objective of the sitting form is to cultivate the mind and health and the objective of the standing form is to train the physical body and its parts. Although there is no proof or evidence, people concluded that the sitting form was created by Zong Li Quan, one of the legendry eight immortals in Chinese mythology and the standing form was created by general Yue Fei in the Sony Dynasty (960-1279) as a martial art gong exercises training to train his soldiers.

Ba Duan Jing developed based on the daoyin principle by manipulate the body and its four limbs to lead the qi circulations to harmonize inside the body. When the qi is in harmony, all the body’s Yin and Yang components are balanced. When the Yin and Yang components are balanced, the body is healthy. A healthy body is a prerequisite for martial art activity. Ba Duan Jin is an exercise divided into eight individual exercises. Through bodily motion from practicing each exercise is to stretch the sinews, vessels, muscle groups, ligaments and tendons in the body so the qi and blood will be better circulated from inside the body to the surface of the body and the physiologic organs will be improved as well to attain good health. Each of the eight exercise is specifically designed to work on the specific part of the body. It is simple to learn, remember, practice and very effective. There are many Chinese martial art styles adapted it as a form of martial art supplementary gong exercises training and health maintenance exercise for their prospective students

Among the Chinese martial arts practitioner community, Yi Jin Jing is a very valuable supplementary gong exercise. It is an exercise training to develop power. Therefore, each style of Chinese martial arts has its Yi Jin Jing variation exercise make available to its perspective student.

What is Yi Jin Jing? It is based on a novel principle in Chinese martial arts training and an exercise created by our ancestors based on the information from Daoist’s Teaching, Buddhist’s Teaching, Hui Tuo’s Five Animals Play, Ba Duen Jin, Daoyin Principle and Tuinan Principle (Inhalation and Exhalation). It is an exercise to transform the tendons and ligaments at the bodily joints and the sinews and vessels in the body. The objective of this exercise is to improve one’s body condition and with the ability to go beyond physical limitation. At the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644), it was the peak of Chinese martial arts development. Chinese martial arts developed into Internal martial art system which emphasized on power development (refining the body) and external martial art system which emphasized on technical development. The training curriculum has forms training, combat simulations training and gong-exercises (fundamentals and supplementary) training. These three types of training are inter-connected. The function of the gong exercises training supplements and provides the forms and combat simulations with preparation. Therefore, the forms training and combat simulations training demonstrate the result of gong exercises training. Forms training can improve the body condition, coordination, flexibility and technique. Body condition, coordination and flexibility provide the combat simulations training with versatile, swift and spontaneous action and reaction. Combat simulations training can elevate and awareness the offense, defense and the understanding of each movement’s offense and defense as well as the coordination among different parts of the body. Awareness adds a great deal to the martial value of the technique. One cannot find this method in other physical activities and sports. Based on the Yi Jin principle (transforming the sinews, vessels and others body parts), there were many exercises developed. It is not simply to improve body health but to develop martial art integral power. Chinese martial arts practitioners recognized that the power generate from the coordination of the ligaments, tendons, sinews, vessels, bones and muscles are more useful and superior than the power generate from the muscles alone in the martial art unpredictable environment. Therefore, if one is able to enhance the condition of the ligaments, tendons, sinews, vessels, muscles and bones, one is able to generate more power. Ligaments, tendons, sinews and vessels are the connective tissues connecting muscles and bones at the bodily joints and throughout the body. Their physiologic functions are to connect the body, muscle groups with the bones and other organs to better support the body to conduct in any physical movement. Therefore, the ligaments, tendons, sinews and vessels stabilize all the bodily joints movements and support body manipulation. They protect and assist body manipulation. One can see, any physical movement is involved the movement at the bodily joint. If one has strong ligaments, tendons, sinews and vessels, the movement will become swift and powerful. Therefore, all Chinese martial arts developed supplementary gong exercises make available at the training curriculum to train the perspective students’ body condition by enhance the condition of the ligaments, tendons, sinews, vessels and more. The names of the exercises might be different according to each style, any supplementary gong exercise with the objective to transform or enhance the body ligaments, tendons, muscles, bones, sinews and vessels is belonging to the category of Yi Jin Jing exercise.

In 1957, The Chinese government recognized and believed that martial art was the cause of violence in society, that the technical application function of martial art had no place in a peaceful society. Government officials began to transform the traditional martial art functions of body cultivation and technical application into Wu Shu competition sport. With this transformation, the new generation of martial art practitioners born after 1957 focused their martial art training simply on forms training, not the traditional three major training areas of forms, combat simulations, and gong exercises trainings mentioned above. With the emphasizing on forms training, one is focused on the technical merit of beauty, difficulty, and high jumping movements, the qualities as competition sport and performing art, not on the practical technique aspect such as simple technique with speed and power. We know that the distinctive feature of martial art is its function as a combat art. Without this function, martial art is no longer a traditional martial art; it is but a calisthenics exercise and a performance art. It is only when one can maintain martial art’s features and complete training curriculum than it is worthy of existing with the possibility of promulgation.

Today, there are many practitioners who do not pay attention to the gong (fundamentals and supplementary) exercises training, no knowledge of them or have no access to acquire the exercises. With different objectives or neglect of the martial objective, these people assume that the martial art forms training and martial art simulations training are the entire Chinese martial arts training curriculum. This is why the contemporary Chinese martial arts practitioners are not as skillful as in the past.

II. Martial Art Form Training

Martial art forms are unique to Chinese martial arts. They serve as the entry level of Chinese martial arts curriculum. They teach students the fundamental information about martial art techniques to exercise the legs, hands and body as well as the coordination among different parts of the body. This is equivalent to calligraphy. First, one follows someone’s calligraphy sampler to learn all the brush strokes and later, write calligraphy without the sampler to develop his/her calligraphy style. Forms have the same function in martial art training. Therefore, one begins with forms training. All Chinese martial arts systems and styles have many distinctive forms. Generally, a bare hand and weapon forms can be done alone, with a partner or with one or more weapons. As a good martial art practitioner, besides executing the offensive and defensive techniques, one should be able to develop a flexible and nimble body, so the hands are capable to move fast and freely; the feet are mobile from the forms training so one is able to retreat or advance easily during martial confrontation.

The development of a good martial art form is the result of many generations of practical and training experiences. A good form has many effective martial art techniques, application and variations. Therefore, a form is a warehouse of many techniques. Generally, a good form is kept secret and not revealed to the public. There are some forms that emphasize strong and powerful technique, and there are others that emphasize soft and yielding techniques. There are forms that only have one or two techniques and there are forms that have over hundred techniques. They all share the similar function of improving the body condition of a practitioner and the fundamentals of martial art.

Today, there are many people misleading the significant of martial art forms, these people spend a great deal of their time to learn forms. After they have learned the bare hand forms, they want to learn the weapon forms. After they have learned the weapon forms, they want to learn the partner forms. After they have learned the Tai Chi Chuan solo forms, they want to learn the Hsing I Chuan forms. After they learned all the Hsing I Chuan forms, they want to learn the Ba Gua Palm forms, etc. They take pride in their knowledge of forms and think the more forms they know, the better. This idea is not correct, especially with immature practitioners. We know there is a limit to one’s memory, time and life expectancy. An immature practitioner has to work daily to make a living. How much time does one have to devote to practice the forms daily? If a person knows so many forms, how much time does he/she has to devote to the practice so he/she will not forget the forms and benefit from them? People practice the forms to improve the fundamentals and body condition, not simply to remember them.

Martial art forms are not the actual combat art. They are but preparation and rehearsal. One learns the use of the body through movement. These movements mimic combat. It is the same thing with dance. One learns to use and control the body through movement to express emotion and artistic value. One also learns to focus so that the mind and body are in unison. But the forms are not as practical as some people expect. Since it is pre-arranged, during practice a practitioner should follow all the rules and techniques from the forms as they were created. This is completely different from martial confrontation in which all techniques are executed based on the opponent's strike or situation. If one applies all the techniques exactly from the forms for martial confrontation, one will be defeated easily by the opponent. If one simply copies the techniques from the forms for martial confrontation, the method is wrong and risky. This is why traditional Chinese martial arts training has a specific training program called disassembling or breaking down the techniques. It is a training by breaking down the movements from the forms to understand all the offensive and defensive techniques from each form’s individual movements.

III. Martial Art Simulations Training

Martial art forms are developed by experienced practitioners. Besides providing an easier method to learn and to remember the techniques, a way to heighten interest, a way to improve coordination and condition, a form can also have many limitations from a practical perspective; for instance, if the movements in a form have been included because of their artistic function and/or personal preference, their application value can be limited and might be misleading. For example, there are many techniques in the forms that happen on the left side without the right side or happen to the front and not to the back or involve the upper body without the lower body. At the same time, to improve the flowing rhythm of the forms, some movements have been added that have no application value. In addition, to highlight artistic value and difficulty in the forms, a practitioner might have to perform some unnecessary difficult movements; actually, in a real martial confrontation, one would not need them. In a martial confrontation, the major characteristics of any technique are: simplicity, speed and power.

An opportunity to strike is available for only a short time. Therefore, one has to execute the strike quickly. If the forms have many techniques and a practitioner goes through the forms just to remember the techniques, one will have spent one’s time for nothing—from a practical perspective. Generally, the forms are composed of many movements and techniques. After finishing the entire form, one would have practiced each technique one, two or three times; however, if one selects a few techniques from the forms and works only on them, after the same amount of time that it takes to go through the forms, one would have practiced these individual techniques ten or more times.

Which method is more efficient for martial art training? The answer is obvious. In order to have certain techniques available in a martial confrontation, one has to select them from the forms and practice these selected techniques separately. This knowledge and practice are called breaking down the form movements. The training is called either the solo drill or the partner drill.

In this training, practitioners disassemble the offensive and defensive techniques from each form movement. One practices these individual techniques based on their offensive and defensive values until one can freely execute them. This training is often called the solo drill. After many hours of practice, one is able to freely execute these techniques in their offensive and defensive contexts.

In the next level of training, a practitioner continues to work on these offensive and defensive techniques with a partner. At the beginning of the training, the partner is often played by the teacher. This second level of training is known as partner drill. In the partner drill, the teacher often plays the role of the defense at the beginning and the student plays the role of the offense. After many times of practice, the student is able to freely execute the strike. The roles change in the next training. Now, the student plays the defense and the teacher plays the offense. When the student is familiar with the execution of the offensive and defensive techniques, the student graduates from this training and the teacher would encourage the student to venture into society to exchange skill with practitioners from other martial art styles to continue his/her training.

Martial art combat simulations training is directly related to martial art confrontation. Besides the execution of the offensive and defensive techniques, it deals with strategy, power delivery, distance, and timing, etc. It requires three training steps. They are the identification of the offensive and defensive techniques, the solo drill and partner drill trainings. Today, there are many people who think martial art forms training are accurate preparation for martial confrontation. There are others who have no knowledge of martial art combat simulations training, supplementary exercise training and then there are others who focus on practicing martial art forms as health exercise, competitive sport and ignore their value as combat art. Martial art combat simulations training and supplementary gong exercises training are the key to martial art success. It requires absolute dedication from the student and a special bonding between the teacher and the student. In our commercialist society, this is very difficult to do.

IV. Martial Art Gong Exercises Training

Martial art gong (supplementary and fundamental) exercises training is supplemented the martial art forms and combat simulations trainings. It is one of the three major trainings curriculum in Chinese martial arts. The gong exercise training is to improve the body condition, the quality of forms, techniques and combat skill. Most importantly, it is the trainings to allow the body’s performance to surpass physiologic limitation. The exercises in the training were developed to improve the practitioner's body condition, technical capability, quality and specific skill such as improve body condition and health, develop the body to possess the ability to resist being injured from strike and increase the intensity of power strike, etc. One generally begins with a simple exercise and progress to a more difficult and demanding exercise.

Martial art supplementary gong exercises training is a unique training curriculum in Chinese martial arts. It is a training to improve and enhance the martial art techniques and skills. This is why people say that if one has no supplementary gong exercises training, it is a waste of time. Supplementary gong exercises training offers different exercises according to each distinctive martial art system and its philosophy. However, the exercises with the objective for fundamentals gong training is similar to all Chinese martial art systems such as enhance the condition and quality of the ligaments and tendons in the body to have better technical performance proficiency. The objective of the supplementary gong exercises is to improve the technical offense and defense proficiency. The exercises are classified into yin gong (hard training), rou gong (soft training), nei gong (internal training), wai gong (external training) and shang gong (light training). The hard training emphasizes conditioning the muscle groups and bones. The internal training emphasizes mind-intent creativity, qi and power development. The external training emphasizes strengthening the four limbs for martial combat. The soft training emphasizes lubricating the joints. The light training emphasizes body control and balance. The exercises from these five groups of supplementary gong exercises trainings are generally divided into empty training and heavy training methods and have two objectives: the primary objective is for defense or developing the invincible body and the secondary objective is offense or how to deliver the strike properly and intensify the striking power.

Although the supplementary gong exercises training has many exercises, each Chinese martial art system developed their own exercises to reflect the system's distinctive philosophy and practice. The unique supplementary gong exercises training helped the practitioners to develop extraordinary skill and power. This cannot be done with the power generated from the contraction and extension of muscle groups alone.

The supplementary gong exercises training includes practicing the bare hand forms, weapons forms, an individual technique, a specific set of exercise to master the coordination of the movement of the eyes, hands, elbows, shoulders, wrists, hips, knees, body position and stepping. These aim to improve the internal power, or body integrated power to strike.

Since the martial art gong (supplementary and fundamental) exercises training is to improve the quality and execution of a technique, the gong exercises training should be composed of the following information:

a. offensive and defensive tactics

b. application and variations of the techniques

c. technical elements of a movement

d. power elements of a movement

e. mechanical elements of a movement

f. mobility and positioning

g. offensive and defensive techniques.

h. Standing meditation

Generally, the gong exercises training is the first step in martial art training or fundamentals training. It yields all the technical values described above. It is also a good method for character development. If one does not spend a great deal of time on these exercises and master all the components involving a specific technique, it is difficult for one to attain higher martial art skill later. Therefore, one must obtain this correct information from a knowledgeable teacher. The correct gong exercises training method, perseverance and discipline are the key for martial art’s training success.

Generally, Chinese martial arts training involves coordination of internal and external attributes. The better the coordination, the better the skill, it is only when one has demonstrated this coordination and unified capability that one will realize which areas need more work. Supplementary gong exercises training functions to improve these weak areas so they will become stronger. Since martial art skill has many levels, what is sufficient at a lower level may not suffice at a higher level, and so one should engage in supplementary gong exercises training at all levels with different exercises.

To acquire any benefit from the supplementary gong exercises training, one has to invest a good amount of time and effort. Skill is the result of daily accumulation. There is no short cut, whatever the objectives of the exercises. Generally, the mechanical motions of the exercise are simple. Therefore, the practitioner has to be patient, persevere, and dedicate himself or herself to the practice routine well, he/she should not afraid to be boredom either.

The three types of Chinese martial arts trainings are different from western sport. A form is generally pre-arranged by a series of movements with offensive and defensive techniques following a specific set of rule or strategy. When one practices the forms, the body is going through a series of manipulation. The manipulation can improve the body condition, the understanding of the offensive and defensive techniques and strategy. The combat simulations training either in the solo drill or partner drill, is to work on the specific offensive and defensive techniques and tactics. The gong exercises training emphasizes on improving the quality and technical of execution. These three types of training are inter-connected. The function of the gong exercises training provides the forms and combat simulations with preparation. Therefore, the forms training and combat simulations training demonstrate the result of gong exercises training. Forms training can improve the body condition, coordination flexibility and the technique. Body condition, coordination and flexibility provide the combat simulations training with versatile, swift and spontaneous reaction. Combat simulations training can elevate awareness offense and defense and the understanding of each movement’s offense and defense as well as the coordination of different body parts. Awareness adds a great deal to the martial value of the technique. One cannot find this method in other sports.

V. Conclusion

Chinese martial arts are considered as a culture by many people. It is the result of its unique training methods, principles, characteristics and contributions to society. It has a long history in Chinese history. The nature of martial art is combat. As a consequence, it developed into many functions today as it incorporated with many traditional Chinese cultures. Although the Chinese martial arts developed into with different features and functions such as technical value, health value and entertainment value, but the core value is still as a combat art. The value of the fundamentals training is the key to improve the overall skill and body conditioning.

The techniques in Chinese martial arts, due to the different in style, have different requirements. Generally, all styles share the followings in common. They are four techniques, eight methods and 12 motions and rhythms.

a. Four Techniques

The four techniques refer to kicking, wrestling, striking and grappling. Every martial art movement has combat value and the movement generally has one or more of these four techniques. Each technique has its own meaning. For example, in kicking, there are many different methods. In striking, there are many body parts involved. In wrestling, there are many ways to manipulate the body to perform the wrestling technique. In grappling, there are many ways and body parts involved.

b. The Eight Methods

The eight methods refer to the training method with the hands, eyes, body, technique, stepping, spirit, essence, qi, power and supplementary gong exercises to arm oneself as a warrior. In another words, it refers to the training of the upper body, head, trunk, lower body, spirit, breathing, power and the skill of the hands, eyes, body, feet, breath, power and technique. Every martial art movement involved with one or more of the kicking, striking, wrestling and grappling techniques and require turning and twisting of the body, using the hands and stepping with the feet. In order to perform these movements well, one must coordinate the eight subjects mentioned above well. Therefore, the movements of these eight subjects cannot perform simply as daily activity but center around martial art activity and value. Under the martial art requirement, the eight subjects should be performed with the following in mind: The fist is fast like a shooting star; the eyes are sharp like thunder; the waist is soft like a moving snake; the stepping is balanced like glue sticking to the ground; the spirit is in its fullness; the qi is sinking; the power travels to the extremity; the supplementary gong exercises should be done with 100% effort.

i. The fist is fast like a shooting star

The hands are light and flexible so that they can move fast and with power. Actually, this is not simply the requirement of the hand but the palms, wrists and fists. In order to fulfill this requirement, the three bodily joints of the wrists, elbows and shoulders should be flexible. One should pay extra attention to exercise these bodily joints.

ii. The eyes are sharp like thunder

In martial art, the eyes do not move by themselves. They generally follow the movements of the hands or the overall movement of each posture. If the hands move but not the eyes, the movement is not good. Therefore, in order for the eyes to follow the hand movements, the neck has to be flexible so it can move quickly to match the hand movements. The eyes also function to reveal and confirm the intention of a movement. It is often say that if the mind is there, the intention is there. If the intention is there, the power will be there as well. For example, when one is performing a forward strike, the eyes should be looking forward. However, if the eyes are looking to the left, the meaning of forward strike is lost.

iii. The waist is soft like a moving snake

Since the body is performing many motions, the body has to be soft and flexible so all the motions can be done. The soft and flexibility of the body is controlled by the waist. When the waist is soft, the body is flexible like a moving snake. This is commonly say that the body should be soft and flexible like water, so it can transform into many shapes based on the container. In here, the container is referred to the opponent’s strikes. The body includes five areas: the chest, back, waist, abdomen and buttock.

iv. The stepping is like glue sticking to the ground

This is the requirement of the lower body. Martial art practitioners often say, "First look at the stepping, then follow up with the hands”. They also say, "It is easy to move the hands and difficult to move the feet." These highlight the role of stepping in martial confrontation. Martial art is a dynamic activity. The parties involving are constantly changing positions to take on the advantage positions to strike. We know that to move the feet quickly and properly are very difficult: they have to be fast, stable and balanced as if they are glued to the ground. The stepping should not be influenced by the movement of the upper body and hands, rather, the stepping of the feet should provide assistance to the upper body and hand movements. People often say that if the stepping is not balanced, the fist strike has no target. If the stepping is not swift, the fist is slow. One can see that the quality of the stepping directly affects the quality of the strike. In martial art, the techniques of the hands, eyes, body and stepping cannot be done separately. They should work together as one unit. The eyes are following the hands and the stepping is following the body.

v. The spirit is in its fullness

This is the requirement of all the internal attributes. This is often interpreted as the fullness of spirit or the spirit is concentrated. If one executes a technique without concentration, the movement looks imbalance, no power and empty.

vi. The qi is sinking

This is the requirement of the breathing. In martial art, breathing is directly related to endurance and power. When one is out of breath from performing the movements, one feels dizzy, lacking balance in the performance of the movements. Therefore, one should practice the deep breathing often. With regular practice, one can lower one’s center of gravity so that one has enough power to finish all the movements with ease.

vii. The power travels to the extremity

In martial art practices, one has to use power and deliver power. Actually, all physical activities use power. Otherwise, when one performs all the movements without accurate power, the performance is like dancing. However, if one does not use power correctly, all the movements look stiff. Therefore, in order to use and deliver the power properly, one should work on the body's three sections to stretch the bodily joints, six harmonies to coordinate all the body parts inside and outside and the present of the four bodily extremities. They are muscles, bones, sinews and blood. It is so by manipulate their extremities. The extremity of the muscle is tongue. The extremity of the bone is the teeth. The extremity of the sinews is the nails. The extremity of the blood is the hairs or head. Specifically, manipulation is done by applied the teeth from the upper jaw and lower jaw close together with the intention to bite off the gums. The tongue touches the roof of the mouth and the tip of the tongue touches the teeth with the intention to push them outside the mouth. The nails from the fingers and toes are bend inward with the intention to have the tips of the finger nails and toes nails penetrate into the muscles. With the combination of the three parts work together, the excitement and fiery emotion reach to the top of the head to activate the blood flow so that the four body parts are presented. Therefore, in order to have a powerful execution, the execution must have the present of the four body parts (sinews, bones, blood and muscles)

The three sections are the upper body, middle body and lower body. The three sections of the upper body are hands, elbows and shoulders. The three sections of the lower body are feet, knees and hips. The six harmonies are the hands, elbows, shoulders, feet, knees and hips

viii. The supplementary gong exercises training should be done with 100% effort

This refers to the quality of the skill. Although the supplementary gong exercises training is important, its aim is to develop power, speed, endurance, nimbleness, proficiency and all the issues relating to the body coordination and technique. However, the supplementary gong exercises mechanisms are simple in nature; they can get boring. Therefore, they require 100% effort from the practitioner. 100% effort refers to patience, perseverance and dedication. When one is dedicated to the training, the quality and skill is assured. This achievement can be attained when one has quality transmission plus quality and quantity practice. People often say that the skill is attained from practice. It is through regular practice that the quality of body condition and skill will be attained. In order to attain quality skill, one should pay attention to the following five areas during practice.

i. Each movement should be properly aligned.

One should follow a specific rule to perform each movement so it is executed properly.

ii. Each posture well structure

Simply having each posture properly aligned is not enough. The posture must be well aligned and positioned so that it supports and stretches the body and sinews. Stretching is the basic requirement to exercise the body to keep fit and the source of internal power.

iii. Inside and outside coordinate

All martial art movements have specific offensive and defensive meanings. When one performs a specific movement, one has to physically demonstrate the meaning by way with the internal coordination. Without the internal coordination and support, the movements lack power.

iv. Continuity

Martial art forms are composed of many postures. When one practices the forms, one should practice them in a continuous fashion without any break. The postures follow each other like a chain in a fluid sequence.

v. Distinguish Yin and Yang Components

In martial art movements, there are the elements of dynamic and static, empty and full, hard and soft, slow and fast, light and heavy, up and down, left and right, etc. One should clearly define them in performance.

c. 12 Motions and Rhythms

It refers to the common 12 types of motions and rhythms. They are dynamic, static, ascending, descending, one foot is standing, two feet are standing, turning, bending, swift, slow, light and heavy.

In martial art activity, there are the dynamic, static, jumping, landing, two feet standing, one foot is standing, turning, bending, fast, slow, light and heavy movements. In order to perform the motions and rhythms well, during the dynamic situation, the motion should be move like the ocean waves, nonstop. The motion should be clear and stable so it has rhythm. In the static situation, the motion is stable like a mountain. In jumping, the motion is nimble like a monkey. In landing, the motion is like a bird landing on a tree-top. In the one leg standing situation, the motion is balanced like a crane standing on one leg. When one stands on two legs, the motion is upright and stable like a tree. When one turns, the motion should be soft, light and flexible so that the turning is like a wheel moving around the axis. During the light situation, the motion is executed with so much control that it is like a leaf floating. During the heavy situation, the motion is heavy like a metal. In fast movements, the motion is swift like the wind blowing. When one is slow, the motion is executed steady like a eagle flying in the sky looking for its prey.

The 24 essential requirements are the basics of Chinese martial arts. In order to perform the material art techniques well and attain good skill, one should keep these requirements in mind and practice them regularly.

Although Chinese martial arts developed into a health maintenance exercise, performance art and competition sport with many functions such as improving one’s emotion, discipline, character development, adaptability, exploring cognition, etc. It is still a combat art. As such, it upholds a very high standard. Although we are living in the 21st century and daily survival is no longer dependent on martial art skill, it still plays a significance role in our daily life.

articles.summary: Tai Chi Chuan is one of the martial art systems. It is also a health exercise that is enjoyed by many people.
articles.content:
I. Introduction

Tai Chi Chuan is one of the martial art systems. It is also a health exercise that is enjoyed by many people. Today, many people refer to Tai Chi Chuan as Tai Chi. This confusion of terms, whether intended or not, is not good for Tai Chi Chuan’s development. Tai Chi Chuan practitioners should understand what each term means.

II. Tai Chi Philosophy

The term Tai Chi first appeared in the Book of Changes better known as Yi Jing, in which, it is said, (Out of Tai Chi is born Two Elements; out of Two Elements are born the Four Phenomena; out of the Four Phenomenons are form the Eight Trigrams.) The term Tai Chi here refers to the originator of everything. Later, in the Northern Song Dynasty, a Neo-Confucian philosopher by the name of Zhou Dun Yi (1017-1073) expanded this notion with the contribution from Daoism. He used the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol to demonstrate the common elements in everything. What he did was make a circle to represent Wu Chi. Inside this Wu Chi Circle, he drew a wave line in the middle separating two equal black and white components to represent Yin and Yang components. The black component represented Yin component and the white component represented Yang component. Inside the white component was a black dot to show that Yin component existed in Yang component and inside the black component was a white dot to show that Yang component is existing within Yin component as well as transformation is happening in the same space and time With this, he established a duality principle to explain that Yin and Yang components are the most basic of all things. When these two components intercourse, everything is multiplied. Later, when this duality principle became popular, people used the term Tai Chi as Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol to represent the universe.

Now, we can see that the term Tai Chi in the Yi Jing (book of changes) does not have the same meaning as the term Tai Chi in the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol. The first one refers to the originator of all things and the second refers to the duality principles.

III. Tai Chi and Tai Chi Chuan

There are many Tai Chi Chuan classics written over the years by skillful practitioners. The most quoted among them was written by Wang Tsung Yueh (1525-1606). It said, “Tai Chi came from Wu Chi, mother of Yin and Yang. When it is in motion, it separates into Yin and Yang. When it is still, Yin and Yang combined.”

Although there are many family styles of Tai Chi Chuan today, their routines and techniques maybe executed differently, their theories and principles are remaining the same. All came from the philosophy from Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol, lao Tzu’s teachings and other. If there is a style or practice that does not follow the philosophy represented by the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol, it is not Tai Chi Chuan.

The relationship of Tai Chi and Tai Chi Chuan are based on the philosophy and experiences. Tai Chi contributes the philosophical component and Tai Chi Chuan contributes the experience component. The symbol demonstrates that when Tai Chi Chuan is in motion, it will divide into Yin and Yang components. This duality principle is exhibited in Tai Chi Chuan as hard versus soft; motion versus stillness; empty versus fullness; open versus closed. Etc.

As a Tai Chi Chuan practitioner, besides practicing the Tai Chi Chuan solo form, one should understand the theory behind it. After all, Tai Chi Chuan is the physical interpretation of the Tai Chi philosophy.

articles.title: Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol
articles.summary: The art of Tai Chi Chuan is based on the philosophy represented by the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol. This Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol came from the Luoshiu, which is a mathematical diagram.
articles.content:
Introduction

The art of Tai Chi Chuan is based on the philosophy represented by the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol. This Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol came from the Luoshiu, which is a mathematical diagram. The story goes that when Xia Yu was assigned to manage devastating flood waters, a mystical turtle carrying a diagram on its shell surfaced from Luoshui. Xia Yu obtained this mathematical diagram and made his own arrangement of it (fig. 1), according to the following:

Wearing the nine and stepping on the one;

Left is three and right is seven;

Two and four are the shoulders;

Six and eight are the legs;

Five is the center.

The rule of this arrangement is that odd numbers are at the four directions and that even numbers are at the four corners and that the sum of opposite numbers equals ten.

How did the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol come from the Luoshui Mathematical Diagram? First, convert numbers into dots, then consider all odd numbers (dots) to be Yang and all even numbers (dots) to be Yin; then connect all the Yang numbers together to form a “S” shape (fig. 2); next, draw a circle to enclose this “S” and we have a two-elements diagram (fig. 3). The Two Elements philosophy developed further to become the Yin/Yang philosophy. In the symbol, the Yang Eye appears within the extreme Yin Fish and the Yin Eye appears within the extreme Yang Fish (fig.4). This is the Yin and Yang Symbol.

In order for one to make better and more fruitful progress in Tai Chi Chuan training, one should spend some time in researching the meanings hidden in this simple-looking symbol. Better known as the “Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol,” it is a circle divided into two equal portions by a wavelike line, with one portion shaded (Yin) and the other unshaded (Yang); the shaded portion has a small unshaded circle in the center of it, and the unshaded portion has a small shaded circle in its center (fig. 5). This symbol can be interpreted as containing the following information, or knowledge, all at the same time and within the same space: opposition and complementarity; one dividing into two and two combining into one; slow changes and sudden changes; transformations of both quantity and quality; inclusiveness and exclusiveness; extreme dimensions from small to large and from large to small; reason and result; matter and spirit; maturity and immaturity.

There are many ways to draw this ancient symbol, according to the location of the two portions and according to whether the spiral rotates in a clockwise or counterclockwise way. The Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol can also be divided into “pre-heaven” (fig. 6), with the Yang component on top and the Yin component at the bottom, and “post-heaven” (fig.7), with the Yin component on top and the Yang component at the bottom, modes. The pre-heaven Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol represents a way to understand nature and uncover universal knowledge and is used to predict the future. The post-heaven Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol is considered a reflection of nature. It has two meanings. One, it gives a clue that humanity’s development is dominated by the Yin component. Within the circle, we see the Yin component is on the left side and the Yang component is on the right side. This indicates the Yin component should be developing upward and forward—which is the objective of humanity. The second meaning contains the recommendation to make thinking ability and strong will, both associated with Yin energy, priorities. Yin energy has no limitation; it is extraordinary.

The observation from this orientation is based on humanity’s perspective. It assumes that the Yang component is visible and has mass and shape, so that one can spend more time in studying it, and that the Yin component is invisible, without mass and shape, and is therefore very difficult to study and understand.

Following are a few of the ways the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol may be represented.

A. Counterclockwise Direction

We often observe the symbol in the following four positions:

a. 12 O’clock

The shaded portion is on the top with the “head” on top and “tail” pointing down to the left. The unshaded portion is on the bottom with the head on the bottom and the tail pointing up to the right (fig. 8).

b. 3 O’clock

The shaded portion is on the right with the head pointing up and the tail pointing down. The unshaded portion is on the left with the head pointing down and the tail pointing up to the right (fig. 9).

c. 6 O’clock

The shaded portion is on the bottom with the head on the bottom pointing up and the tail on the bottom pointing down. The unshaded portion is on the top with the head pointing down on the left and the tail on the top pointing down to the right (fig. 10).

d. 9 O’clock

The shaded portion is on the left with the head pointing to the left and the tail pointing up to the right. The unshaded portion is on the right with the head pointing up to the left and the tail pointing down to the left (fig. 11).

B. Clockwise Direction

We often observe the symbol in the following four positions:

a. 12 O’clock

The unshaded portion is on the top with the head on the top and the tail on the bottom pointing to the right. The shaded portion is on the bottom with the head on the bottom and the tail on the top pointing to the left (fig. 12).
b. 3 O’clock

The unshaded portion is on the right with the head on the right pointing down and the tail pointing up. The shaded portion is on the left with the head pointing up and the tail pointing down (fig. 13).

c. 6 O’clock

The unshaded portion is on the bottom with the head pointing to the left and the tail on top pointing to the left. The shaded portion is on the top with the head pointing to the right and the tail at the bottom pointing up to the left (fig. 14).

d. 9 O’clock

The unshaded portion is on the left with the head on the right pointing up and the tail pointing down. The shaded portion is on the right with the head pointing down and the tail pointing up (fig. 15).

Interpreting the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol

Tai Chi comes from Wu Chi. Wu Chi is the state of being void. It then separates into two, or heaven and earth. Heaven and earth have four seasons. Each season is divided into hard and soft, or Yin and Yang. When we arrange these four seasons with their yin/yang components, they became the Bagua Diagrams, or eight trigrams. A trigram composed of three lines: upper line represent heaven, the middle line represent humanity and the bottom line represent earth. One can see that the creation of the Bagua Trigrams was the result of the ancient Chinese studying the universe. The trigrams represent an understanding and explanation of the relationships among what is found in nature.

In order to explain the basic building blocks of nature, the ancient Chinese classified them into eight characteristics or phenomena. They are heaven, earth, wind, thunder, water, fire, mountain, and swamp. Everything in nature evolved based on the interaction of these eight characteristics or phenomena. Each trigram represents one of these eight, and is composed of three lines, either straight or broken. A straight line represents the Yang Characteristic and a broken line represents the Yin Characteristic. The arrangement of these three lines dictates the meaning of the trigram. Chien, Kun, Chen, Ken, Li, Kan, Tui, and Sun are the names of the eight trigrams in Chinese. Although the formations of the trigrams are important in relationship to their meanings, it is difficult to remember them, so The Neo-Confucianist philosopher Zhu Xi (1130-1200) came up with a song based on these three-line formations:

Chien is three continuous; kun is six broken.

Chen is an upward cup; ken is an overturned bowl.

Li has an empty middle; kan has a full middle.

Tui is deficient on top; sun has a broken bottom.

The Bagua Trigrams can be arranged into the pre-heaven diagram (fig. 16) and the post-heaven diagram (fig. 17). The pre-heaven diagram begins at the top with Chien, followed by Sun, Kan, Ken, Kun, Chen, Li, and Tui; it contains the meaning of opposite characteristics in nature. The post-heaven diagram begins at the top with Li, followed by Kun, Tui, Chien, Kan, Ken, Chen and Sun; it contains the meaning of complementarity and correlation.

Today, we often see a Bagua Diagram composed of a Tai Chi Symbol at the center surrounded by the eight trigrams. It does not matter which variation of the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol we draw within the Bagua Diagram. However, for the post-heaven Bagua Diagram, which people often use to interpret life’s events, it is most proper when the shaded portion (Yin) is at the bottom and the white portion (Yang) is at the top.

A. Four Features of the Symbol

In studying the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol, one must begin by clarifying the four most important components of it: the outer circle; the Yin and Yang “Fishes”; the fish eyes; and the wavelike line that divides the circle into two.

a. The Outer Circle

When one looks at the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol, the first thing that greets the eyes is the outer circle. The ancient Chinese often used the circle to represent heaven, with its characteristic of continual transformation, whereas the square was used to represent earth and its characteristic of stability. In the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol the circle represents both heaven and the universe.

From a philosophical perspective, people often use something tangible that everyone can witness, such as a drawing of a circle, to represent something intangible that needs to be imagined, such as circulation, transformation, and progression in life. Here are a few ways we can look at the circle:

i. The circle represents everything that exists in a circular pattern. In life, there is the cycle of birth, growth, maturity, and death. In the universe, the earth is constantly orbiting the sun; the stars also move in orbit. This natural phenomenon is unstoppable.

ii. The circle represents everything that exists primarily in a round bodily shape. All life forms on earth exist mainly in round bodies, as do all the planets.

iii. Circles are closely related to spiral movement, which represents activity. Activity is the basic characteristic of the universe. Since the circle represents the active universe, everything that exists in it should be spiral in nature. Herein lies the secret meaning of the circle.
Tai Chi Chuan practitioners understood the secret meaning behind the circle. The centripetal and centrifugal forces resulting from circular motion will repel or neutralize any threat. Therefore, all the Tai Chi Chuan solo form movements have both circular and square motions, reflecting the quality of Yin and Yang, and this quality is distinctive in every movement, so that all the movements are soft, continuous, even, and connected with the others in a balanced—stable—way. The Tai Chi Chuan Classics state, “All the movements flow like the ocean’s waves, one after another.” When one is practicing the Tai Chi Chuan solo form, one should make sure to have this information in mind.

b. The Yin and Yang Fishes

In the pre-heaven Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol the circle is divided into two equal portions that look like two fishes. The shaded portion is called the Yin Fish and represents inactivity; the unshaded portion is called the Yang Fish and represents activity. They are the same size, and the head of one is connected to the tail of the other. This drawing represents an active yet stable body.

When, as is common, the symbol is drawn in a horizontal alignment, the Yang Fish on top represents heaven, the Yin Fish at the bottom represents earth, and the middle represents people. In Yin and Yang Theory, the universe is composed of Yin and Yang elements. Those which are bright, above, active, and hard are considered to be Yang; substances which are dark, below, inactive, and soft are considered Yin. In this way, everything that exists in nature can be classified as either yang or Yin. It is said that Yin and Yang is the principle of heaven and earth, the foundation of all things, the originator of life and death. If one does not understand basic yin/yang theory, whatever one does—or does not do—is already a mistake.

In teaching Tai Chi Chuan, the instructor often repeats what he says over and over by way of stressing the importance of this Yin and Yang Theory. He or she might emphasize the importance of having a soft and relaxed body at the same time as having firm and solid feet. The soft and relaxed body reflects heaven’s characteristics of openness and emptiness, which enable the practitioner to react in different ways according to the situation: turning and twisting the body, moving fast or slow, with hardness or softness, etc. Having firm and solid feet reflects earth’s characteristics of solidity and thickness, which support and endow the practitioner with mobility and the capability to execute movements such as kicking with ease.

When one is able to understand Yin and Yang Theory and incorporate it into one’s Tai Chi Chuan practice, one can then progress quickly with his/her skill. Understanding Yin and Yang Theory is very important in Tai Chi Chuan practice.

i. Yin and Yang opposition: In this interpretation everything exists in two components that are opposite from each other, as with Yin and Yang. They do not exist equally with each other in one unit; rather, they are constantly struggling to overtake each other within the same unit. It is this constant struggle that sets everything in motion.

ii. Yin and Yang complementation: In this interpretation the two components coexist in one unit, depending on each other to survive. Neither Yin nor Yang can survive by itself: if there is no right, there cannot be a left. Therefore, the Yang component relies on the Yin component to survive and vice versa. Each component needs its opposite in order to exist. If this Yin and Yang harmony is disrupted, neither component will be able to survive.

iii. Yin and Yang balance: In this interpretation Yin and Yang are not equally divided. Each is constantly struggling to overtake the other. Sometimes there is more Yang than Yin and other times more Yin than Yang. It is this constant state of struggle, however, that enables them to live together. An example can be shown using the four seasons. In the summer there is more Yang than Yin, while in the winter, there is more Yin than Yang. In the year as a whole the Yin component and the Yang component remain equal to each other. Although they are complementary, one should not overlook the importance and significance of balance. Everything must exist in a balanced state in order to grow and prosper.

iv. Yin and Yang interaction: In this interpretation Yin and Yang are constantly in opposition and struggling to overtake each other and grow. Therefore, at certain times Yin becomes Yang and Yang becomes Yin as they evolve and reproduce in this constant state of interchange. The result is transformation in terms of quality—from quantity. This interchange—transformation from one to the other—occurs when they have reached maturity.

The Tai Chi Chuan Classics say that Tai Chi comes from Wu Chi. When Wu Chi takes an active form, it divides into two parts. When it is in an inactive form, the two come together as one. With the symbol’s division into its Yin and Yang components, Tai Chi Chuan’s physical movements begin, in accordance with the philosophy of the symbol in its active state. Therefore, one should expect to see Yin and Yang components existing everywhere in the Tai Chi Chuan solo form. In Tai Chi Chuan practice, one can discern yin and yang components manifested in the following ways: left-hand and right-hand interactions; extension and contraction of muscles; coordination of top and bottom; harmony of inside and outside; opening and closing movements; up and down movements; empty and full stances; left and right eye movements; active and inactive states of the mind. Each couple is happening at the same time.

c. The Fish Eyes

In the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol there is a small black circle inside the Yang Fish and a small white circle inside the Yin Fish. In our discussion we have explained that Yin and Yang can be complementary, opposed, balanced, and interacting, as well as existing everywhere; the key to these transformations lies in these “fish eyes.” There are several meanings behind them.

i. The fish eyes demonstrate that nothing is absolute in this world, that everything that exists is composed of many levels.

ii. The fish eyes explain that the original source of transformation of an object comes from within the object itself.

iii. The fish eyes explain that everything has a logical progression. Things generally begin in infancy and progress to adulthood, moving from weak to strong. It is a process that nothing—or nobody—can stop or disrupt.

iv. The fish eyes explain that each thing that exists has its own source of power. Everything has opposite and complementary components within.

v. The fish eyes represent a condition of either imbalance or balance within a larger body. For example, when a body is healthy, all the organs function normally, with order, coordination, and stability. The Yin and Yang Fishes explain the body’s healthy condition. The fish eyes explain balances and imbalances among the individual internal organs and systems.

vi. The fish eyes explain the relationship of people to the environment. They show how one should be in harmony with and utilize the environment.

vii. The fish eyes represent the infinite process of division.

There are two ways to draw the location of the fish eyes. In the first one (fig. 18), the eyes are located next to each other as in left and right—the location of Kan and Li in the Bagua Trigrams. This representation shows a complementary relationship. It is simple and nice, and has a sense of dynamic motion. Besides the complementary relationship, it includes the principle of harmony as well as the idea of imbalance within balance.

In the second drawing (fig.19), the fish eyes are located one on top of the other—the location of Chien and Kun in the Bagua Trigrams. This represents heaven and earth as well as good health and longevity.

In martial art terms, if there is all Yang without any Yin, the technique is rigid, lacking variation; it is not a good technique. If there is all Yin without any Yang, the technique is too soft and does not have any fighting power; one will end up on the defense the whole time. If a Yang technique also contains Yin, it will have visible power; if a Yin technique also has Yang, it will have hidden power. A good technique combines the two for a powerful strike.

Today, many people who practice Tai Chi Chuan overemphasize softness and relaxation. They demonstrate overly soft movements that are reminiscent of cooked spaghetti. Obviously, this interpretation of Tai Chi Chuan practice is not correct; Yang Characteristics are lacking. A martial art technique must have both Yin and Yang elements in order to be powerful enough to cause serious devastation. Therefore, in Tai Chi Chuan practice, one should keep in mind the importance of balance, stability, and progression.

d. The Wavelike Line

This wavelike line in the Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol separates Yin and Yang in spiral motion. It signifies that the transformation of all things is continuous without break or end. The earth takes one year to complete an orbit around the sun. People on earth observe the sun orbiting from the east to the west. The moon takes one month to complete its orbit of the earth, also from west to east. In the past, because people often observed the sky while facing south, they concluded that the universe was turning to the left or that it turned from the right to the left.

In the Tai Chi Symbol, if the Yang Fish is in the upper left corner and the Yin Fish is in the lower right corner, this makes the spiral motion inside the symbol move toward the left—i.e., the universe is turning to the left. We can see this observation represented in Tai Chi Chuan practice in five ways:

i. Traditionally, the practitioner faces south at the beginning.

ii. The solo from always begins on the right side, moves to the left side, and ends on the right side.

iii. To do the form correctly, one must rotate the waist in every movement.

iv. All the movements are executed with dynamic circular motion.

v. The circular motion should have varied speeds.

Conclusion

The Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol is but one piece of the Chinese cultural heritage, resulting from precise and insightful observations on the part of ancient Chinese philosophers. Although it is a simple-looking symbol, the Yin and Yang Theory that it represents summarizes all natural phenomena, transformations, and correlations; it reveals secret information about nature’s relationships, transformations, and growth. This hidden information is brilliant. It contains constructive creativity, precise observations, clear insights, and inspiration.

Tai Chi Chuan is an art of physical movement created by ancient Daoist practitioners to reflect and interpret this philosophy. Therefore, many questions related to Tai Chi Chuan practice can be answered by studying this Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol.
