articles.summary: Of all the countries in the world, China has the largest population, with fifty-six different ethnic groups, and the fourth largest land mass. Geographically, the northern, higher landscape is flat, and the southern, lower landscape is hilly.
articles.content:
I. Introduction

Of all the countries in the world, China has the largest population, with fifty-six different ethnic groups, and the fourth largest land mass. Geographically, the northern, higher landscape is flat, and the southern, lower landscape is hilly. With all its diversity, the economic development, customs, culture, and architecture in each area are very different. Therefore, the martial-art styles that people practice in the many different areas have their unique features. The different styles of Chinese martial art developed as a result of the differences in culture and customs in the different areas. The northern people are built physically different from the people in the south. Therefore, the martial art styles in the north have more of an emphasis on long-range strikes and incorporating the legs in their techniques. The martial-art styles in the south have more of an emphasis on short-range strikes and incorporating the hands in their techniques.

Chinese martial art has a long history and has developed into many styles. Although there are many styles, they are commonly divided into internal and external Chinese martial art systems. Within the two systems, there are differences in objectives, strategies, values, requirements, training methods, and results. Many people understand that Tai Chi Chuan belongs to the internal Chinese martial-art system. Why is Tai Chi Chuan an internal Chinese martial-art style? What is the difference between the internal Chinese martial-art systems and the external Chinese martial art-systems? In this article I would like to share with readers my understanding concerning these issues.

II. Tai Chi Chuan Emphasizes Mind-intent, not Physical Power

In Chinese history, Chinese martial art became divided into external and internal systems at the beginning at the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644). One should know that both internal and external Chinese martial-art systems have advantages and disadvantages. One cannot and should not claim that one kind of system is better. The differences lie in a practitioner’s skill achievements: how dedicated a practitioner practices and trains, how deep his/her understanding is of the art he/she is engaging in, the personal preference of a practitioner regarding the style he/she is interested in, etc.

Generally speaking, external Chinese martial art systems developed first. One of the reasons for this is that the method of power application is similar to that in daily activities. It is common practice to apply power while performing any specific project, whereas it is the opposite practice in the internal Chinese martial art systems, which require one not to use any power. Therefore, an external Chinese martial-art system is easier for people to study, understand, and master. The author of The Art of Internal Art Techniques, Huang Bai Jia (1643-1709), said that Zhang San Feng, who lived in the Song Dynasty (960-1279), changed the external system to come up with the internal system and that Wang Tsung Yueh (1525-1606) summarized this in The Tai Chi Chuan Classics:

This art has many options; although the techniques are different, most of them represent the strong bullying the weak, the slow defeated by the swift. This is the result of natural ability, not of physical science.

From this quotation, we understand that Zhang San Feng changed the source of martial art power from natural ability to something more scientific, relying on a human being’s three treasures: essence, qi, and spirit, so that when one is executing martial-art techniques, they are no longer based on natural ability or physical strength but on scientific knowledge. This change was a milestone in the development of Chinese martial art.

Tai Chi Chuan, as an internal Chinese martial art style, requires at the beginning of its training that the student not use any physical power. This is completely opposite of people’s daily habit of applying power. Actually, this requirement has confused many people, causing doubts and questions. They reason that any physical activity requires power to be exerted. How can one not use any power? In addition, since Tai Chi Chuan practice is done so slowly and softly, is it really possible that it can function as a fast and powerful martial art? These questions refer to the issue of power application. Today, we understand that with the advancement of scientific technology power can be applied in many ways and that different functions are involved. The principles of “soft overcoming hard” and “one ounce overcoming a thousand pounds” are completely different from the external martial-art systems’ techniques of power application, which emphasize the principle of “more power, the better.”

The source of power in internal Chinese martial-art systems is very different from the source of power in external Chinese martial art systems. Internal Chinese martial-art systems apply neijin, or internal power, and external Chinese martial-art systems apply natural ability, or physical power. For the development of the neijin power source, the method of training is called “applying mind-intent creativity and qi circulation.” It involves the three treasures of a human being, and the product is called neijin, or internal power. The method of training in external Chinese martial art systems is called “power training.” It involves strengthening the physiological organs’ capabilities, and the product is called “natural ability.” Therefore, the method of focusing on mind-intent creativity and qi circulation, rather than strengthening natural ability, is for training neijin. It is this neijin power source that distinguishes internal from external Chinese martial-art systems.

One may ask: without power, how can one execute techniques? We know that executing any movement requires power; this is obvious. The answer lies in the type of power source. External Chinese martial art systems use natural ability, or physical power, and internal Chinese martial art systems use neijin, as mentioned. One can develop this second type of power with genuine instruction from a knowledgeable instructor. Otherwise, the training is in vain, and Tai Chi Chuan practice is but a calisthenics exercise in which all physical motions are fueled by natural ability, not neijin. This is why Tai Chi Chuan practices have to be guided by so many abstract principles—because the ingredients for Tai Chi Chuan neijin are intangible. It is difficult to understand and develop.

After one obtains the genuine transmission and invests the time to practice, it is guaranteed that one will achieve neijin, and the body will be filled up with neijin. With neijin as the power source, any part of the body can be applied as a weapon, and one becomes able to apply the principle of “static to defeat dynamic.” The amazing result is that, although the body seems to be not making any movement, as soon as the opponent makes contact, he/she will be bounced away; or, when one is discharging the neijin, a small movement of the hands or any other part of the body will send the opponent flying off several feet. Since the discharge of this neijin requires only a small physical movement, Tai Chi Chuan uses this neijin as an energy source to fuel its application techniques. Therefore, Tai Chi Chuan is considered an internal Chinese martial-art style.

III. The Difference between Internal and External Chinese Martial Art

Today, when people discuss Chinese martial art, it is often divided into external and internal systems. Buddhist martial art, or the Shaolin martial art style, is referred to as an external Chinese martial art system. This is so because practitioners execute the techniques in a fast and powerful way. One is able to apply the techniques after a short time of training. In addition, one employs the strategy of “strike first.” Daoist martial art, or Wudang martial art style, is referred to as an internal Chinese martial art system. This is so because practitioners execute the techniques in a slow and relaxed manner that appears to be without any power. One has to spend a much longer time in training before one can apply the techniques, which have internal and external attributes. One employs the strategy of “strike second.” Obviously, this is a simple and incorrect classification of martial art systems, and there are many of them. Over the years, the classification of Chinese martial art systems has caused many controversies. Shaolin is the name of a Buddhist monastery in Henan Province, and Wudang is the name of a mountain in Hubei Province. To construct a better way of classifying martial art systems, one should have a better understanding of the meaning of external and internal martial art systems and how they relate to offensive and defensive martial art techniques.

There is a common statement that goes, “Internally, one is developing qi; externally, one is developing sinews, bones, and skins.” There is another statement that goes like this: “One Yin and one Yang is called martial art.” Yin refers to all the attributes in the body that one cannot see; Yang refers to all the attributes in the body that one can see. A third statement goes, “The application of a martial art involves the presence of qi and physical movement.” This statement means that the effective execution of any martial technique must coordinate the qi power source with bodily movement.

Qi has many names and definitions; it has been extensively researched throughout Chinese history. We know that a physical movement generally involves the sinews, bones, and joints of the body. Sinews have the ability to extend, contract, accumulate, turn, twist, and expand, and they are connected to the skeletal system. The bones and joints have a structure-support capability, as well as being able to turn, twist, and contract. People often refer to these functioning capabilities of the sinews as “sinew power,” and the functioning capabilities of the bones and joints as “bone power.” All the kinds of physical movement are the result of this sinew power and bone power.

Although the statement goes, “The application of martial art involves the presence of qi and physical movement,” there are many different levels of coordination between qi and physical movement. If in a martial-art system qi rather than physical movement dominates in the execution of techniques, this system emphasizes qi for fueling all the techniques. If in a martial art system physical movement rather than qi dominates in the execution of techniques, this system emphasizes natural ability for fueling all the techniques. These two types of martial art systems are different with reference to skill level, external features, styles, and results. Therefore, these should be the criteria for the classification of internal and external systems in Chinese martial art. We can say that a system in which qi fuels the techniques is an internal Chinese martial art system, and a system in which natural ability fuels the techniques is an external Chinese martial art system. Therefore, an internal Chinese martial art system should have the following four unique features.

a. It is not based on a neigong training exercise.

It does not matter whether a style is an internal Chinese martial art or an external Chinese martial art, as long as it is an independent, complete Chinese martial art system, generally the style will have one or more set of neigong (internal work) and waigong (external work) training exercises for martial power in addition to its solo form training. The Shaolin martial art style is known as an external Chinese martial art system; besides its waigong training exercise, it has its neigong training exercise as well. The Wudang martial art style is known as an internal Chinese martial art system; besides its neigong training exercise, it has its waigong training exercise as well. Thus, there are many Chinese martial art styles that have both neigong and waigong training exercises. One cannot conclude that external Chinese martial art systems do not have neigong training exercises or that internal Chinese martial art systems do not have waigong training exercises. The difference between the internal Chinese martial art systems and the external Chinese martial-art systems is not based on neigong training exercises or waigong training exercises. It is based on neijin. Therefore, the concepts and definitions of neijin and neigong are not the same.

b. There is a difference in power application.

For external Chinese martial art systems, in order to increase the power going to the hands, the practitioners generally make an inhalation first to channel the power from the waist and hips to the shoulders, then from the shoulders to the arms and hands. When the power is channeled to the hands, one can actually observe vibrations in the extremities. In the past, practitioners tied the waist with a belt after inhalation to perform this process better. (This function has evolved to become a symbol of rank in Japanese martial art.) In addition, they worked very hard on the lower body to establish stability, because the power manifested at the hands is rooted in the lower body. This process of channeling power is very visible. When the strike is launched, it looks very powerful and fast.

In internal Chinese martial art systems power is applied in a way opposite to the way it is applied in external Chinese martial art systems. The qi sinks down to the dantien, three inches below the navel. The Tai Chi Chuan Classics say,

The root is at the feet, discharged from the legs, controlled by the waist, and manifested at the fingers. From the feet to the legs to the waist—it is connected as one unit.

“One unit” refers to the qi circulation. Therefore, one does not pay attention only to a specific or selected part of the body. When one attains higher skill, it is possible for the neijin to go wherever the mind-intent orders.

In external Chinese martial art systems, the power is channeled upward to the hands, and in internal Chinese martial art systems the qi sinks downward to the dantien; or, in external Chinese martial art systems the waist sinks to establish stability, so the hands can function to discharge power, and in internal Chinese martial art systems the qi sinks downward to the dantien for attaining unity, so that top and bottom are coordinated. One part moves followed by all parts moving together, with the mind-intent rather than physical power being applied to manage bodily movement. This is the major distinction between the two kinds of martial art systems. In other words, when one is feeling that the power is in the hands, this is an external Chinese martial art system. When one is not feeling any power in the hands, this is an internal Chinese martial-art system. When one achieves higher skill in Tai Chi Chuan, one cannot see any physical movement when discharging power. This is why Tai Chi Chuan is called an internal Chinese martial art system.

c. The focus is not on the techniques.

Today, there is a surge of interest in Tai Chi Chuan, and the demand for Tai Chi Chuan instruction is very high. Instruction has become so widespread that one can obtain it almost anywhere. There are Tai Chi Chuan classes offered in local community centers, commercial health clubs, health and wellness centers, as well as martial art schools for those people interested in it as a martial art. When it comes to martial-art instruction, students generally begin with learning a series of movements called the “form.” There are many types of forms: it can be a bare-hand form, a weapons form or a two-person form. A form practice by one person is called solo form and a form practice by more than one person is called a partner form.

After one learns the forms, the next step is to identify the offensive and defensive techniques within these forms. This is called “assimilation training,” and it is an important part of a martial-art training curriculum. It involves a process of breaking down a specific movement from a form in order to identify all the offensive and defensive techniques. Without this process, a practitioner does not know how each movement is applied in a combat situation. However, since Tai Chi Chuan uses neijin as its power source, executing the physical movement is but secondary when it comes to application. With neijin behind a movement, any simple movement can and will become a powerful martial technique. Therefore, an internal Chinese martial art system like Tai Chi Chuan generally does not focus on assimilation training but instead focuses on developing jin power—dongjin skill—in its curriculum. This is why people spend so much time on the Tai Chi Chuan push-hands exercise practice; it is for developing dongjin skill.

In Tai Chi Chuan, each movement has obvious offensive and defensive techniques. This is true. It is the result of the choreography of the martial-art form. If there were no form to practice, it would be very difficult to begin this exciting and challenging journey. Understanding the techniques in each movement assists practitioners to properly execute the movement correctly, deliver power efficiently, and correctly manipulate the body. These are the major ingredients in martial activity. Therefore, practicing the form represents martial-art fundamentals training for improving body condition, martial knowledge, and awareness. All the benefits and martial techniques are derived from practicing the form. As one can see, without form to practice, it would be difficult to engage in martial-art training—developing and improving one’s skill.

When one trains the body to become soft like water by practicing the form movements, one is able to easily apply the body in offensive and defensive techniques. Applying the body is simply the result of understanding the body’s Yin and Yang. When the body is filled up with neijin, any part of the body that comes in contact with the opponent can be applied as a weapon either to yield and neutralize the threat or to offer a counterattack, automatically. Therefore, for these spontaneous defensive and offensive maneuvers one cannot find correspondences to any form movements. However, any movements in the form or any parts of the body in the form movements can be used to apply offensive and defensive techniques. The amazing results of these swift offensive and defensive maneuvers are the function of body integration. For beginning students without firsthand experience, this is difficult to understand.

d. It involves applying the waist.

In our daily life, we usually perform most of our tasks with the movement of the hands; this movement is not incorporated with the rotation of the waist. If we were to ask someone to incorporate the waist in performing a task, mostly likely we would receive a negative response. With internal Chinese martial art it is highly recommended to incorporate the waist and then have the waist lead the four limbs in each movement.

The waist is located at the midsection of the body. It serves three unique functions. It is a control center for all physiological activities, a connector for upper and lower body coordination, and it enables, from its unique position, the entire body to move in a steady manner. This can be better understood from the following example. Let’s assume that we are grasping the center of a spider’s web and shaking hard; the vibration will transmit evenly throughout the web from the center to the edge; if, however, this action does not originate from the center, the vibration will not be transmitted evenly throughout the web. There are many people who do not understand this recommendation. They say that it violates the daily habit of power application. Applying the waist is the essence of internal Chinese martial arts. It is opposite to one’s daily habit. Searching for the opposite is the interpretation of the principle of the dao reversing in Lao Tzu’s teaching. Breaking the habit is the change that Zhang San Feng made. It is this different understanding that makes it difficult for many practitioners to progress. When one is practicing an internal Chinese martial art without incorporating the waist in each movement, the result is no body unity.

The waist is the connector of the upper and lower body. If the waist is not relaxed (loose), it is difficult to have power integration, which is rooted in the feet and manifested through the hands. Without power integration, one ends up with the power being discharged solely from the hands. The intensity of this kind of power discharge is not so great.

When one has a relaxed waist, the form practice consists of having the waist make circles, or circular motion. With regard to the limbs, one can reach out to make “big circles”—big circular motions—or to make “small circles”—small circular motions, all these motions being based on one’s own wishes. In addition, when the waist is relaxed, the arms are able to reach out farther and one is able to efficiently utilize the elbows as weapons.

When one truly attains waist relaxation, one will discover that one’s previous form practice was actually inauthentic most of the time, with the four limbs making too many independent movements or too many secondary bodily motions and not enough primary bodily motions. In other words, the practice has not been natural enough. When one truly knows how to apply the waist, one’s understanding and practice will become more detailed, nimbler, slower, and versatile—complete. As one can see, continuing with Tai Chi Chuan practice will lead one to search for more information, acquire more knowledge, and become more intelligent.

IV. No Circle Neijin in Tai Chi Chuan

In addition to the differences mentioned above, internal Chinese martial art system is emphasizing the training of the body and the body’s condition. This kind of training is better known as harmonizing the internal attributes: of heart and mind-intent, mind intent and qi, and qi and power; and the external attributes: of shoulders and hips, hands and feet, and elbows and knees. The external Chinese martial art system is emphasizing the training of controlling others. With this difference in emphasis, internal Chinese martial art systems pay closer attention to all areas of the body, the body’s condition, and the mechanics of bodily movement.

Although everybody knows that smooth bodily movement is due to the structure and function of the body’s joints, practitioners of internal Chinese martial-art systems understand that smooth bodily movement is the result of the joints functioning in circular motions and of better quality of the joints: the better the quality, the smoother the movement. Since the joints play such a significant role in the quality of bodily movement, internal Chinese martial art practitioners have done much research on the bodily joints and human anatomy. They have come to understand that the body is divided into three sections and each section is sub-divided into three sections. Therefore, the body’s nine sections are connected by nine joints. The joints for the body’s middle section are along the vertebrae (cervical, thoracic, and lumbar). The joints for the upper section are the wrists, elbows, and shoulders. The joints for the body’s lower section are the hips, knees, and ankles. One should study the anatomy of the body’s joints and exercise them well in order to maximize the range of motion for each joint.

When a joint is involved in a large motion, it is called a “big-circle” motion; if a medium motion, it is called a “medium-circle” motion; if a small motion, it is called a “small-circle” motion. When one makes the biggest motion one can, it is so big that there is no more space outside this circle. When one makes the smallest motion, it is so small that there is no space inside it. In other words, these two phenomena are known as no more circular motions or “no circles.” They are but two points.

The progression of Tai Chi Chuan skill should begin with big circle, or big circular motions, and go on to small circle, or small circular motions, and finally end with no circle, a point. When one practices the Tai Chi Chuan movements with expansive motion to stretch the body and joints for martial art fundamentals training, it is derived from the big circular motion or big circle principle. When one practices the Tai Chi Chuan solo form movements with compact motion to refine and rehearse the agility and automatic response for swift action during martial engagement, it is derived from the small circular motion or small circle principle. In terms of discharging power, small circle is referring to the skill of capable to discharge one-inch power to a one-centimeter power and big circle requires more body parts involvement. This classification refers to the distance across which one is capable of discharging power efficiently. In push hands exercise, when power is applied but not seen, and the opponent is thrown back several feet, this is the result of one possessing the capability of discharging power at a very short distance. Although discharging power is generally associated with physical movement, experienced Tai Chi Chuan practitioners are able to deliver power with minimum movement. Therefore, Tai Chi Chuan is called an internal Chinese martial art. The discharge of power is invisible.

This special skill in Tai Chi Chuan of delivering power with minimum movement, or, as it is called, “no-circle neijin application,” is very different from the “hidden power” that many people know about. This hidden power has minimum involvement with connective tissues and bones when the power is delivered at the contact area; therefore, it is called hidden. There are many people who can execute this hidden power. There are two obvious differences between hidden power and no-circle neijin. First, with hidden power, besides the body parts that are directly involved, all others parts of the body cannot move; whereas in Tai Chi Chuan’s no-circle neijin, all parts of the body are moving in unity. Second, neijin happens only as the impact area makes a “static-controls-dynamic” action. Although this action is small, it is made with body integration, so it is very powerful. Whereas the hidden power is often applied when one delivers it at the time of competing, and the body is very stiff; this action is not capable of pushing the opponent very far backward.

When one applies this no-circle neijin in Tai Chi Chuan push hands exercise correctly, it demonstrates what The Tai Chi Chuan Classics call, “No feather can be added and no fly can land.” During contact, although it may be just a very small amount of power from the opponent— as light as a feather—one can still deliver enough neijin to neutralize the opponent and to bounce his/her body far off. Although one can hardly see any external movement, the opponent’s threat is already neutralized and being bounced off. When one has neijin, any part of the body has fajin (discharging power) capability. This is often called, “the entire body has Tai Chi.” Any part of the body that makes contact with the opponent can be applied as weapon. During the execution, the movement is so small that one cannot see how it is happening. Therefore, Tai Chi Chuan is called an internal Chinese martial art style.

V. Conclusion

The concepts of internal and external Chinese martial-art systems were introduced for the first time in 1669 by Huang Zong Yi (1610-1695) on the tombstone of his friend Wang Zheng Nan (1616-1669).

The Shaolin martial-art system is famous. Although its emphasis is on controlling the other, it has flaws. There is an alternative system called internal art. It applies the static to control the dynamic. An opponent falls down as soon as there is contact. This is different from the external Shaolin system.

Huang’s son, Huang Bai Jia, wrote in his book The Art of Internal Style Techniques, which was published eight years later, after his teacher, Wang Zheng Nan died:

The external Shaolin system is excellent. Zhang San Feng was very good with this system. He made some changes in the system, and it is called the internal system.

Although Huang Zong Yi did not provide further information about the internal Chinese martial art system, applying the tactic of “static to control dynamic” and “the opponent falls down as soon as there is contact” provided enough clues to understand that this internal Chinese martial-art system does not emphasize natural ability, rather the profound neijin skill behind the techniques.

In order to emphasize the profound neijin skill behind the techniques, one has to train the body so well that it is flexible and versatile, as if there were no bone. When the body is flexible, one can manipulate it according to the opponent’s action and apply the principles of centrifugal and centripetal forces to defeat the opponent. This is similar to the nature of water, which naturally takes the shape of the container it is in. In this case, “the container” is the opponent’s action. In order to accomplish all of this—not an easy task—experienced practitioners have developed many theories, principles, and training methods for future practitioners on this exciting and challenging journey. This is why an internal martial-art style such as Tai Chi Chuan takes longer time in training to attain skill.

Among the different theories and principles, Yang Cheng Fu’s “Ten Points” provides good guidance for beginning students engaged in Tai Chi Chuan training. They are: suspend the head from above; sink the chest and raise the back; relax the waist; differentiate insubstantial and substantial; sink the shoulders and point the elbows downward; use the mind and not physical force; upper and lower coordinated; inside and outside harmony; connected without interruption; and seek stillness in action. Plus, the training method of push-hands is invaluable for developing sensitivity, neutralization, listening, discharging-power skill, etc.

When one engages in Tai Chi Chuan practice for some time, guided by many training methods and incorporating of Yang Cheng Fu’s “Ten Points,” one is able to demonstrate genuine internal martial-art skill—a unique skill. The unique skill I am referring to involves the following.

a. When one has practiced internal Chinese martial art for a while, one’s power-application skill will begin with one-inch power, advance to one-centimeter power, and, finally, attain the sensitive skill of “no feather can add and no fly can land.” In fajin application, one hardly sees any physical movement, yet the opponent is already bounced several feet away.

b. One is capable of applying the principle of “static to control dynamic”: without any obvious physical movement the opponent is thrown back several feet immediately after contact.

c. The entire body has fajin capability, resulting from attaining the skill of no circle, or, the entire body is Tai Chi. Any part of the body making contact with the opponent can function as a weapon to defend oneself and to bounce the opponent off several feet.

Chinese martial art has many styles and each style has its unique features and training methods. After one obtains genuine transmission and invests in the time to practice, one will, with dedication, attain the above skill from Tai Chi Chuan training. It employs the tactics of victory from transformation, slow to defeat swift, retreat to advance, weak to defeat strong, and soft to overcome hard, the philosophical concept of Lao Tzu’s teachings of reversing is the Dao, which means that everything in this world is developing in the opposite direction. Tai Chi Chuan techniques are often launched from a static condition when the opponent is in a dynamic condition; applying this tactic, using the static to control the dynamic, conserves power and makes it easier to hit the target. Employing the strategies of “strike second but reach the target first” and “yield to the threat then follow up with a strike” makes Tai Chi Chuan an outstanding representative of the internal Chinese martial-art systems.

Tai Chi Chuan is an excellent martial-art style for demonstrating the development of Chinese martial art. It represents a milestone in this development. Tai Chi Chuan broke down many people’s understanding about martial art. Previously, people believed that martial art is a combat art, nothing else. One had to be strong and single-minded in order to be successful. Besides functioning as a martial art, Tai Chi Chuan also functions as a health-maintenance exercise, an exercise that cultivates one’s temperament, heart, and soul. It is available to people of all age groups and physical conditions, not solely belonging to those with strong physical conditions. It provides an alternative way of applying power, so it is very scientific. This is why millions of people worldwide practice Tai Chi Chuan today.

articles.title: Why Practice Tai Chi Chuan Slowly
articles.summary: There have been many answers to the question of why Tai Chi Chuan is practiced slowly. One answer says that because all Tai Chi Chuan movements are circular, it takes a longer path and therefore more time is needed travel from point A to point B.
articles.content:
I. Introduction

There have been many answers to the question of why Tai Chi Chuan is practiced slowly. One answer says that because all Tai Chi Chuan movements are circular, it takes a longer path and therefore more time is needed travel from point A to point B. Another answer says that when it is done slowly, the practitioner can pay more attention to the mechanical movement. These answers are like a common example of the four blind men who wanted to find out what is an elephant. Each blind mind is to describe an elephant based on what part of the elephant they touched. Regarding to the slow practice of Tai Chi Chuan, I think the reasons are as the followings.

The development and practice of Tai Chi Chuan are following Lao Tzu’s teachings, information from Tai Chi Yin and Yang Symbol, Chinese martial art principles and others. Lao Tzu written in the Dao De Jing chapter 25, “Humanity follows earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows Dao and Dao follows nature.” In chapter 64, he wrote “The size of an embracing tree begins with a single seed. The nine levels stage begins with the accumulation of soil. Ten thousand miles begin with the first step.” These two quotations implied that Dao is invisible, takes time, experience and patience to discovery its true meaning. Dao exists before heaven and earth and its operation is non-stop. It is the root and rule of everything in their existence and activities. This natural Dao is highly emphasized to following the origination and the process of following is happened in a progressive manner. It is not recommended to be in a hurriedness and short cut to get something done quickly. Experience and patient are the correct way to make progression according to the natural Dao. This unique feature of practice externally would be “slowness”. Slowness provides an environment and opportunity to experiencing and understanding. Since following the natural Dao is one of the recommendations by the Tai Chi Chuan classics during practice, therefore, Tai Chi Chuan practice is highly observed “natural” and “slowness’ in its practice. It is a method of feeling and understanding practice, not to be in a hurriedness to get it done quickly practice. Practicing Tai Chi Chuan is a personal experience by applying a calm and tranquil mind set to feel, realize and confirm.

In Tai Chi Chuan practice, slow has two meanings. It is referring to how much time need to complete a Tai Chi Chuan solo form and it is also referring to how much time need to complete a motion in a solo form movement. A movement is referring to the body is moving from point A to point B or from one’s own center of gravity to the opponent’s center of gravity. Therefore, in any effective martial engagement, there should be two motions in a practical technique. Generally, one motion is from point A to point B (first contact the opponent) and the second motion is from point B to the opponent’s center of gravity, point C. The motion from point A to point B is conducted in circular motion due to the body’s anatomy restriction. The second motion (it is from point B to C) is often conducted in a smaller circular motion or close to a square motion so the power is able to penetrate in to the opponent’s body quickly. However, in order to refine the body and its parts involve with the motions, one would increase the size of a circular motion to stretch or exercise the different components in training and reduce the size of the circular motion for application among the internal Chinese martial art styles. This is why one often heard the statement, beginning with big circle and ending with small circle. Since external Chinese martial art is based on natural ability, it does not require and refine the different components in the first circular motion. Since Tai Chi Chuan is one of the internal Chinese martial art styles, it is highly emphasis on refining the body. Therefore, Tai Chi Chuan practitioners often say that skill begin with big circle and end with small or no circle and experienced Tai Chi Chuan practitioners often said that circular motion is for qi circulation and square motion is for the jin power delivery. Since internal Chinese martial art recommended train for power, not technical value, its power source is sufficient to penetrate into the opponent’s body. Since external Chinese martial art recommended the natural ability and technical value, not power, its power source is insufficient to penetrate into the opponent’s body.

Slowness in Tai Chi Chuan practice has specific requirement. It is a speed requires alertness and not wondering or has stagnation. If the slow motion show only stagnation and not lively, it is not a correct slow motion. Therefore, the status of slowness in Tai Chi Chuan should have lively mental activity and vibrant qi. Slowness is a training method for Tai Chi Chuan practitioners to work on the body’s Yin and Yang components to attain Yin and Yang balance. Otherwise, it is difficult for one to aware the condition and manage the body’s Yin and Yang components during their martial art activities’ dynamic conditions.

Tai Chi Chuan is the physical interpretation of the philosophy of Tai Chi. As such, it has Yin and Yang components in the body. Since Tai Chi Chuan is an internal Chinese martial art, as in all Chinese martial arts, it has to provide the best training method to prepare the students to become martial art warriors. The curriculum of the training method is divided into two categories. They are composed of gong (benefit from effort) training and ji (technical) training. Gong exercise training refers to the training of internal power or neijin and ji exercise training refers to the training of body condition or martial art techniques. In another words, gong exercise is focused the training on the circular motion and li exercise is focused the training on speed with square motion.

II. The Two Training objectives

We know that power and technique are the most important parts of martial art skill. Without either one of them, a practitioner’s skill is not high and practicing it but a waste of time to a martial art practitioner. Traditionally, martial art practitioners go to a great length to improve these two areas, go as far as to injury one’s own body from training.

We often hear people say that power is invincible, it can destroy all things and defend against all techniques. We also commonly hear the concept that one ounce can overcome 1000 pounds. These two statements contradict each other and have created confusion and controversy among martial arts practitioners. This is especially true among beginning practitioners in Tai Chi Chuan. In order to become a better practitioner, it is necessary for one to clarify these two vital yet differing ideas about technique and power in martial art practice. When people said "Power is invincible, it can destroy all things and defend against all techniques", this meant when one is in a martial confrontation, power plays a very important role in winning. It also refers to the kind of power behind the training. “One ounce overcome a 1000 pounds” is referring to the technical mastery. Power alone cannot win a battle. Technique refers to a physical movement that can deliver onto the opponent's body. In the past, a material-art technique is defined as a movement capable to contact with the opponent’s body. Otherwise, it is but a physical movement, not martial art technique.

A martial art confrontation consists of competition in power, technique and strategy. The outcome of a confrontation will be determined by a number of factors, including: who is stronger, who has a more powerful and speedy strike, who is more familiar with and able to execute the techniques correctly, and who is able to seize the opportunity. In another words, who is better prepared. These are also the elements the practitioner should focus on in training. Among these elements, power is the sine qua non. If there is no power, it does not matter how good the techniques are or how much experience one possesses, it will all be useless because the techniques alone cannot cause enough harm.

At the same time, in martial-arts practice, power or lack of power is not the only issue. Also at the issue is how to apply techniques properly in martial art’s constantly changing situation of martial-art confrontation. In other words, one must apply techniques effectively so the power is behind in each technique. All martial art practitioners agree that power development or acquisition is the key to martial art's training. Throughout Chinese history, martial arts practitioners have gone to great length to obtain this guarded information and knowledge.

In Tai Chi Chuan training, gong-exercise training is on the internal power development. It is a training involves with elements from the spirit, mind intention and qi, as well as the combination with physical movements to have the body and its parts functions to end up performing task beyond physical limitation. When one is training on the technique or ji exercise training, it is focusing on the applications and variations of the eight techniques of warding off, roll back, press, push, pull down, split, elbows strike, shoulders strike and the Wuxing five elements of left, right, forward, retreat and center and the importance of how to properly deliver their power and directions.

III. Tai Chi Chuan Application

Tai Chi Chuan is one of the cultural treasures of China’s heritage. It has a long history and contains a vast body of information. It was created and developed during thousands of years of China’s long and turbulent history. It is old and it is new. It is elegant and it is simple. It has valuable merits in the fields of self-defense, performance art, health-maintenance exercises, and personal development. It is based on ancient Chinese philosophy, traditional Chinese medicine, martial art, the art of nurturing life, daoyin principles (dao means manipulating the body to become soft and flexible: yin means guiding the qi to be in harmony with the body), tuinan principles (inhalation and exhalation), and more. It has a unique training method, profound principles, and practical applications. Therefore, it does not matter whether it functions as a martial art or as a healing art, Tai Chi Chuan is very different among its peers.

During practice, Tai Chi Chuan emphasizes control and guidance from the heart and the mind-intent over physical movement, sinking the qi, relaxing the body, calming the mind, and deep and slow breathing in its practice. With its specific combination of the coordination of hands, body, and feet movements, according to martial-art requirements, with daoyin and tuinan principles, Tai Chi Chuan became a martial art featuring inside/outside coordination—also known as the internal martial-art style. This combination follows the law of nature, so the body relaxes, lightens, and becomes softer and the body is more in harmony with nature. When one is regularly practiced Tai Chi Chuan in this manner will contribute great benefit to one’s body central nervous system, digestive system, circulatory system, respiratory system, muscular-skeleton system, and immune system.

Tai Chi Chuan developed at the peak of Chinese martial art development. Therefore, it has the most extensive and effective training programs, practical strategy, profound principles and multiple benefits. The feature of martial art is spontaneity. This means during the martial engagement, one is constantly changing from position to position or from technique to technique so one cannot tell the direction and power as any moment. However, one can keep track of the changing from the tangible positions and techniques. Since executing a technique is happened in a short time, participant spend most of the time on changing the position and technique. Therefore, changing is the genuine of martial art activity. Tai Chi Chuan recognized this feature and offering the unique training based on this changing by refining the body to become soft as water or on body condition and power development, not on technical development to support this changing feature. Therefore, the eight major techniques are also known as the eight major jins (internal power) among the Tai Chi Chuan practitioners.

Although each of the individual eight techniques is different technically, they are different in objective and target. Each one utilizes the shoulders, hands, elbows, knees, feet, hips and head. They are known as the seven stars. Generally, because the power of these strikes is issued outward by the movement of the bodily parts as weapons to strike, the eight techniques, also refer to the eight internal powers (eight jins). The Wuxing Theory (five elements) is defined as advancing and retreating of the body and feet techniques; left and right refer to the eye movements and center refers to the body technique or upright positioning. When one has upright positioning, one has balance and mobility and mobility is the soul of martial-art activity and it is also the soul of changing.

Tai Chi Chuan is a martial art and very efficient as such because it applies internal power to fuels each technique. Therefore, when one is practicing Tai Chi Chuan, one is working on the development of internal power by body coordination and integration. It is a special kind of qi power supporting the martial art’s vigorous and versatile movements. The skill and the intensity of this internal power is obtained from relaxed, slow, circular motion, tranquil and soft unique Tai Chi Chuan practice. It is very different from most Chinese martial art styles that people practice today. The movements are done hard, fast and powerful. This is why Tai Chi Chuan is called the internal Chinese martial art style and its practice yields so many benefits, including the benefits from both as a martial art style and as a health maintenance exercise. Like hard style qigong of external Chinese martial art styles, it can develop the facility for taking a powerful punch to the body. But along with taking punches in a stationary posture, Tai Chi Chuan practitioners can take them not only from a stationary posture but in dynamic condition as long as the body is filled-up with internal qi, no harm can be done to the body. This is equivalent to the basketball filled-up with air. One can bounce it as many times as one wishes without rupture it.

As a martial art style, Tai Chi Chuan is able to work together with different parts of the body to issue internal power outside the body to affect other people or bounce people off with a strike. This power is the result of a combination of yielding power and discharging power. Therefore, it can be said that if one does not have this yielding power and discharging power skills, one neither practice Tai Chi Chuan correctly nor attain Tai Chi Chuan martial art skill.

In addition, mind intention plays a very important role in Tai Chi Chuan practices. It is the commander of all movements. It is said in the Six Harmonies Theory that when the mind intention is there, the qi is there and the power is there as well. A movement without mind intention is nothing. Mind intention without movement is likewise nothing. Mind intention combined with movement that is not applied onto an opponent is nothing. When mind intention combined with movement together is applied onto an opponent, something significant is achieved.

A beginner who moves from movement to movement without paying attention to each movement’s value and function is not considered to be practicing Tai Chi Chuan. It is merely calisthenics. Slow motion and relaxed manner Tai Chi Chuan practice provides the needed opportunity for the practitioner to improve.

IV. How to practice Tai Chi Chuan Slowly?

The object of practicing the Tai Chi Chuan movements slowly is to attain Yin and Yang components balance inside the body to perform body integration and coordination. Slowness is one of the features of Tai Chi Chuan practice and it is distinctive different from others Chinese martial art styles. Therefore, Tai Chi Chuan is called the internal Chinese martial art style. Since slowness is mandated by Tai Chi Chuan's feature, in each movement, motion is beginning from the bottom of the feet, then traveling through the feet, controlling by the waist, discharging from the back and manifesting at the hands in this coordinated manner to establish unification and integration. If a movement is done quickly, it is difficult to have this integration, coordination and control. Therefore. one can see, slowness is but a training method and attaining body integration is the objective. There are eight benefits resulted from slow Tai Chi Chuan solo form practices.

A. It is easier to lead the practitioner to have calm and tranquil mind set so that one can focus better in practice

B. It is easier to let the physical and spiritual bodies relax

C. It is easier to have the mind intention control the physical movement

D. It is better to have qi circulation

E. It is better to develop internal power

F. It is better to have the body balance, coordinate and control

G. it is better to stretching and exercising the body

H. it is better for the body to relax

Since slowness is so important in Tai Chi Chuan, how to correctly practice Tai Chi Chuan's movements slowly? I believed there are five options to assist in slowing down one’s practice of Tai Chi Chuan solo form's movements.

A. The mind has to be calm, tranquil and the body should be relaxed. If the mind is not sufficient and tranquil, it is difficult to have the body relax enough to execute the movement slowly with control. Calm, tranquil and slow are complemented to each other. If a person is not calm and tranquil, the eyes are searching. It is impossible to focus; when this is happened, how can a movement be done slowly? Therefore, one can see that the beginning posture in Tai Chi Chuan solo form is very important. It prepares the practitioner to have a calm and tranquil mind sets so one can relax the body to execute each movement correctly with full attention throughout the entire practice session.

B. When all the movements are done naturally, the body is relaxed. Relaxation and slowness are working to together. It is the same coin with two sides. During practice, if the body relaxes, each part of the body's motion involving with a movement should be done with proper rhythm and standards. Keeping it in mind that one should not force into a position. This is not natural.

C. When practicing Tai Chi Chuan, let the mind intention guides the physical movement so that each movement has rooting. It is said that the external physical movement is the reflection of the internal qi circulation. Qi circulation is leading by the body movement. Body movement control by the mind intention activity and the mind intention is control by the heart. Therefore, the quality of the heart is very important. This is why people often said that Tai Chi Chuan is an art involved with physical and spiritual practice. Spiritual practice is the training of the heart by daily experience.

D. In executing each movement, there is a short pause between each movement (physically it is pause but the mind intention is continued). This helps to stabilize the movements by distinguish empty and full body’s weight, and the circular motion from the square motion in each movement. In addition, it improves the coordination and understanding between qi circulation and internal power delivery. A well define movement comes from slow practice.

E. The stepping should be very light and nimble. One should not step forward until all the body's weight is fully shifted onto the supporting leg to distinguish empty from full body weight. To establish this control, one has to begin with a slow motion.

V. Conclusion

The fact is that, when one practices Tai Chi Chuan solo form with mind intention controls, the speed has to slow down. Although practicing Tai Chi Chuan associates with slowness, Tai Chi Chuan does not mean slow. Slowness is but a method of training, not an objective. Indeed, there are many Chinese martial arts also have forms and gong-exercises (supplementary exercises) done slowly to attain the similar objective of fundamentals training. Although most of the time people observe Tai Chi Chuan movements done slowly, it is but personal preference Tai Chi Chuan movements can be practice quickly as well and there are many fast Tai Chi Chuan solo forms available. Otherwise, Tai Chi Chuan is not practice as a martial art style but simply as a calisthenics exercise. Since martial art is a very dynamic and vigorous physical activity, a strong and healthy body requisite. In application, all martial art techniques are done quickly and powerfully in order to be effective. In application, rather a practitioner can or cannot perform the Tai Chi Chuan movement quickly is a question of dedication and transmission. It has nothing to do with the art itself. There is a saying that practice the movement slowly is to train for fundamentals and practice the movement quickly is for application. We are living in a civility society today. Martial art engagement rarely happened. In this peaceful time, people preferred the slow motion Tai Chi Chuan practice for health over the fast motion Tai Chi Chuan practice for martial application.

When one is practicing Tai Chi Chuan solo form slowly, one focuses on the Yin component training or gong exercise component. When one is practicing Tai Chi Chuan solo form quickly, one focuses on the Yang component training or ji exercise component. The Yin and Yang Theory said that Yin or Yang component by itself cannot survive. It is said in the Tai Chi Chuan Classics that when one is practicing the solo form slowly, one is training on the martial fundamentals. When one is practicing the Tai Chi Chuan solo form quickly, one is training on the martial application. The Tai Chi Chuan Classics also said that a practitioner mastered the art of Tai Chi Chuan only when one has mastered both Yin and Yang components and attained Yin and Yang interaction.
